{{Short description|Australian-British nuclear physicist (1930–2021)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
'''David Maurice Brink''' {{postnominals|country=GBR|FRS|size=100%}} (20 July 1930, [[Hobart]], [[Tasmania]], [[Australia]] – 8 March 2021, [[Oxford]], UK)<ref name=obitOxford>{{cite web|url=https://www.physics.ox.ac.uk/news/obituary-david-brink-frs|title=Obituary: David Brink FRS|website=University of Oxford, Department of Physics|date=17 March 2021}}</ref><ref name=NuclearPhysicsNews/> was an Australian-British nuclear physicist. He is known for the Axel-Brink hypothesis.<ref>{{cite web|author=Brink, D. M.|title="Giant resonances in excited nuclei." In: Talk presented at the workshop on chaos and collectivity in many body systems at the PMIPKS, Dresden, March 5-8. 2008|url=https://www.mpipks-dresden.mpg.de/~ccm08/Abstract/Brink.pdf}} [https://www.pks.mpg.de/~ccm08/announcement.html list of workshop's invited speakers] Peter Axel (1923–1983), a professor of physics at the University of Illinois, worked independently of D. M. Brink. [https://physics.illinois.edu/people/memorials/axel In Memoriam: Peter Axel, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]</ref>

==Education and career==
Brink matriculated in 1947 at the [[University of Tasmania]], where he graduated with a B.Sc. in physics in 1951.<ref name=CV>{{cite web|title=CV David Brink - School of Physics & Astronomy|website=website of Ian James Douglas MacGregor, University of Glasgow, July 2012 (Click on "David Brink" for automatic download of CV to user's computer — the download will remain until the user deletes the downloaded file.)|url=http://www.physics.gla.ac.uk/~ianm/epsnpb/organization/activities/meitner/2006/meitner_2006.html}}</ref> As a [[Rhodes Scholar]], he became a graduate student in physics at [[Magdalen College, Oxford]], where he received his PhD in 1955.<ref name=CV/> His doctoral dissertation ''Some aspects of the interactions of light with matter''<ref>{{cite thesis|author=Brink, D. M.|title=Thesis. Some aspects of the interactions of light with matter|year=1955|website=Oxford University Research Archive|url=https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:334ec4a3-8a89-42aa-93f4-2e54d070ee09}}</ref> was supervised by [[Maurice Pryce]].<ref>{{cite web|title=David M. Brink|website=Physics Tree|url=https://academictree.org/physics/peopleinfo.php?pid=838829}}</ref> From 1954 to 1958, Brink was a Rutherford Scholar of the [[Royal Society]].<ref name=obitOxford/> For the academic year 1957–1958 he was an instructor at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT). From 1958 to 1993, he was a Fellow of [[Balliol College, Oxford]]. At the [[University of Oxford]], he was from 1958 to 1988, a university lecturer and from 1988 to 1993 a Moseley Reader.<ref name=CV/> In 1993 he moved to [[Trento]], Italy. There from 1993 to 1998, he was the vice-director of the European Centre for Theoretical Studies in Nuclear Physics (under the auspices of the [[European Centre of Technology]]), as well as, at the [[University of Trento]] a professor of the history of physics.<ref name=obitOxford/><ref name=CV/>

Brink was a visiting scientist at Copenhagen's [[Niels Bohr Institute]] in 1964. He has been a visiting professor at the ''Institut de physique nucléaire d'Orsay'' (1969 and 1981–1982), the [[University of British Columbia]] (1975), the [[Technical University of Munich]] (1982), the University of Trento (1988), the [[University of Catania]] (1988), and [[Michigan State University]] (1988–1989).<ref name=CV/>

As a theoretical physicist he did important research on "the study of nuclear structure via the [[Nuclear shell model|shell model]] and effective interactions, and nuclear reactions via statistical methods."<ref name=NuclearPhysicsNews>{{cite journal|journal=Nuclear Physics News|volume=31|year=2021|issue=3|page=39|title=In Memoriam: David M. Brink (1930–2021)|author=Bonaccorso, Angela|doi=10.1080/10619127.2021.1954452|bibcode=2021NPNew..31...39B |s2cid=237507451 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

{{blockquote|He was interested in the physics of [[giant resonance]]s and developed semi classical methods for heavy ion reactions which he used to explain the selectivity in the population of high angular momentum states in heavy ion transfer reactions and neutron transfer to bound states. His book ''Angular momentum'' (with [[G. Raymond Satchler|G.R. Satchler]]) is a classic introduction to the topic.<br />For several years David had a very productive collaboration with Dominique Vautherin, Marcel Vénéroni and their colleagues at Orsay on the use of Skyrme's effective interaction for [[Hartree–Fock method|Hartree-Fock calculations]] and, later, on the semi classical theory of collective motion in nuclei.<ref name=obitOxford/>}}

He was elected in 1981 a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sukumar |first1=C. V. |last2=Bonaccorso |first2=A. |date=2022 |title=David Maurice Brink. 20 July 1930 — 8 March 2021 |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |volume=73|pages=65–83 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.2022.0020 |s2cid=252091114 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2301.02907 }}</ref> He received in 1982 the Rutherford Medal of the [[Institute of Physics]]. He was made in 1992 a Foreign Member of the [[Royal Society of Sciences in Uppsala]]. In 2006 he received the [[Lise Meitner Prize]] "for his many contributions to the theory of nuclear structure and nuclear reactions over several decades, including his seminal work on the theory of nuclear masses using Skyrme effective interactions, nuclear giant resonances, clustering in nuclei and quantum and semi-classical theories of heavy-ion scattering and reactions."<ref>{{cite web|title=Past winners previous years|website=EPS Nuclear Physics Division - Lise Meitner Prize, European Physical Society|url=https://www.eps.org/page/NPD_prizes_LMeitner}}</ref>
